articles.title: Australian investor home lending plunges 32% in Q3 as tax curbs and RBA hikes bite harder
articles.desc: A drop in home lending this sharp gives the RBA more evidence that its five hikes this year are biting. That supports the case for a pause after November’s split decision, and it is a modest headwind for the Australian dollar. Short-dated Australian government bond yields may be sensitive to any fur
articles.content: A drop in home lending this sharp gives the RBA more evidence that its five hikes this year are biting. That supports the case for a pause after November’s split decision, and it is a modest headwind for the Australian dollar. Short-dated Australian government bond yields may be sensitive to any further sign that housing is cooling faster than the central bank expects. Bank stocks face slower mortgage growth, especially in investor lending, which has traditionally been a profitable segment. With energy-driven inflation still the RBA’s main worry, oil prices remain the swing factor for whether housing weakness is enough to keep rates on hold. - Tax changes, lending caps and five rate hikes have all hit Australian property investors at once, and the result is a collapse in landlord borrowing. Summary: Australian home loan values fell 15.5% q/q in Q3, against expectations of an 8% drop and a 5.2% fall in Q2 Investor lending plunged 32.3%, after falling 10.2% in Q2 Owner-occupier loan values fell 5.3%, after a 1.9% fall in Q2 The May budget ended negative gearing for established homes bought after budget night and curbed the capital gains tax discount APRA has capped high debt-to-income lending since February, and the RBA has hiked five times this year to 4.85% The value of new Australian home loans fell 15.5% in the September quarter, nearly twice the 8% decline economists had expected, as lending to property investors collapsed in the wake of government tax changes and a year of Reserve Bank of Australia rate hikes. Investor lending was the main drag, plunging 32.3% on the quarter after a 10.2% fall in the June quarter. Owner-occupier loan values fell a more modest 5.3%, following a 1.9% decline previously. The overall drop was a sharp acceleration from the 5.2% fall recorded in the prior quarter. The split between investors and owner-occupiers suggests policy is doing much of the work. In the May federal budget, the government moved to end negative gearing for established homes bought after budget night, keeping it only for newly built properties, and also announced curbs to the capital gains tax discount on established dwellings. Negative gearing lets investors offset rental losses against other income. The government argued the housing market needed rebalancing, with most investor credit going towards existing homes rather than new supply. The major banks moved quickly to reflect the changes in how they assess investor loan applications, reducing borrowing capacity for many landlords. Those measures came on top of tighter lending rules. From February, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority required banks to limit new loans at six or more times a borrower’s income to 20% of new mortgage lending, measured separately for owner-occupiers and investors. Monetary policy has added further pressure. The RBA has raised its cash rate five times this year, in February, March, May, September and November, taking it to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, as it fights inflation that has been pushed higher by energy costs. The November decision was split 6-3, and the statement dropped earlier language about further increases. The RBA’s own November Statement on Monetary Policy had already flagged a steep fall in investor lending, describing the drop in investor loan commitments as the largest in any hiking cycle on record. Governor Michele Bullock said a pullback in investor demand was normal in a housing downturn. The bigger fall compared with owner-occupiers, though, suggests the budget changes are having an effect. The figures strengthen the case that housing is cooling quickly, which may feed into the RBA’s assessment of whether its tightening has gone far enough. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Subscription Fatigue: The Paid Tech Services Worth Keeping
articles.desc: A longtime tech user explains which paid subscriptions still earn their monthly cost, from a comic reader and torrent seedbox to a games service and web hosting plan.
articles.content: Subscription Fatigue: The Paid Tech Services Worth Keeping | Technology Subscription Fatigue: The Paid Tech Services Worth Keeping A longtime tech user explains which paid subscriptions still earn their monthly cost, from a comic reader and torrent seedbox to a games service and web hosting plan. Subscription fatigue is pushing many tech users to cancel paid services, but one long-time subscriber says a small group of them still justify their monthly cost. The subscriptions cover comic reading, torrent downloading, mobile gaming, and web hosting, and the author describes them as the low-key services that support daily hobbies and work. Without them, the author says, a large share of day-to-day computing would fall apart. The author draws a clear line between headline entertainment services, such as Disney+ and Plex, and the quieter tools that run in the background. The list of keepers was assembled after a deliberate review of every recurring charge, with each one judged on whether it delivers consistent value. Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features Panels is a comic reader for iOS that costs $1.49 a month or $14.99 for a full year. The author switched to Panels after discovering that Chunky, a free reader, was no longer supported once digital comics moved from iCloud to a personal server running Komga. Panels was chosen over established publisher apps from Marvel, DC, and Japanese platforms such as Shonen Jump. The author says those options and the free alternative offered slow or nonexistent updates. Panels, by contrast, receives more frequent updates and works with OPDS (Open Publication Distribution System), a standard that lets the author deliver files to the app without much hassle. The author also points out that Komga's built-in reader runs through a web browser and looks unattractive. Panels fills the screen with the comic on an iPad or iPhone, with minimal distractions. The app now also supports a range of independent comics that can be streamed directly within it. According to the author, Panels has worked without any issues for around two years and was incredibly easy to set up. The only regular task that involves Komga is updating it with the titles being read. Seedr and Apple Arcade Fill Specific Gaps Seedr is billed as a seedbox and costs $19.99 a month for 2TB of online storage plus a built-in torrent client. The author relies on it to download old video games and historical software from the Internet Archive, which provides torrents for peer-to-peer downloading that can be faster than direct downloads. Seedr keeps downloads running on its own servers, so a personal computer does not need to stay on or restart the torrent repeatedly. Files that the system already recognizes as acquired by other users may be cached on Seedr's end and download automatically, which the author says can take only minutes for ROM sets and BIOS files used by retro systems. Recent updates also added storage at no extra cost and a 'Version 2' of the web app that works much like a typical online cloud file system. The author holds an Apple One subscription, but the service most valued is Apple Arcade. Some games on Apple Arcade are adapted from the App Store into '+' variants without ads or microtransactions, while others are new to the platform. Titles such as Block Blast!+, Balatro+, and Bloons TD 6+ can be downloaded without extra costs or heavy advertising. The author says Apple Arcade has largely replaced the wider App Store as a source of games, with the exception of popular gacha titles. A recommended pick from the catalogue is Grindstone, released in 2019, which suits a commute or casual play while watching television. iFastNet Hosting Remains Essential for Projects The author has kept iFastNet for web hosting since 2019, paying $10 a month for a low-cost web server with unlimited storage and bandwidth. articles.title: New opening date for huge Willesden Aldi store and exact time when doors open
articles.desc: Willesden’s new Aldi store at 473 High Road opens on November 26, with Paralympic medallist Louise Fiddes cutting the ribbon.
articles.content: New Willesden Aldi store exact opening date confirmed | Ham & High New Willesden Aldi store exact opening date confirmed This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. The official opening date has now been set for Willesden's huge new Aldi store. Initial reports based on the store locator on Aldi's website was that the supermarket would open on the former B&M site in Willesden High Road on November 12. But the doors will now open on Thursday, November 26, at 8am with four-time Paralympic hero Louise Fiddes cutting the ribbon. The store at 473 High Road will be managed by David Murray and run by a team of 30 staff. The sign outside the new Aldi reveals that the store which will share the site with a B&M. Mr Murray said: "We can’t wait to open the doors to the new store in Willesden. "It’s set to be a special day and having Paralympic hero Louise Fiddes join us will make it a morning to remember." Fiddes will also hand out free bags of fruit and vegetables from Aldi’s Super 6 range to the first 30 customers in the queue. She said: "I’m so excited to be opening Aldi’s new store; it will be great to chat to customers and a lovely way for me to thank Aldi for its support of ParalympicsGB." The new store will offer a full range of Aldi’s products, including fresh British meat, its Specially Selected range, exclusive beers, wines and spirits, and a Food to Go section. The site was previously a Homebase then a B&M store which closed in March 2025. Aldi bulldozed the old store and has been working since December to rebuild two new stores side by side on a larger footprint with a 96-space car park. The second store will be occupied by a B&M, although it is not known when the store will open. Aldi has been named the UK’s Cheapest Supermarket for 2025 by consumer group Which? for the fifth consecutive year. The brand is encouraging Willesden charities and food banks to register with Neighbourly, a platform that connects businesses with local organisations in need of support. Charities that sign up will be able to collect surplus food and perishable items, including fruit, vegetables and baked goods, seven days a week. The company is inviting any interested charities in the area to get in touch via aldi@neighbourly.com. The new store will be open Monday - Saturday: 08:00 - 22:00 and Sunday: 11:00 - 17.00. articles.title: Zero tariff on agri exports to Japan pushed
articles.desc: SEN. Francis Pangilinan said zero tariffs on Philippine agricultural exports to Japan could create more opportunities for Filipino farmers. Pangilinan, chairman of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Food and Agrarian Reform, joined Sen. Erwin Tulfo in advancing the proposal. It was raised during t
articles.content: SEN. Francis Pangilinan said zero tariffs on Philippine agricultural exports to Japan could create more opportunities for Filipino farmers. Pangilinan, chairman of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Food and Agrarian Reform, joined Sen. Erwin Tulfo in advancing the proposal. It was raised during the Philippine Senate delegation’s official visit to Japan, which coincides with the 70th anniversary of Philippine-Japan friendship. During the visit, Pangilinan said that the country should not focus solely on domestic food production but also work toward opening larger international markets for Filipino farmers and fisherfolk. “We cannot focus all our resources on being food producers alone. We also need to pour in all our efforts into opening bigger markets for our farmers so they can have better and bigger opportunities to improve their livelihoods, increase their incomes, and secure their and the country’s future,” he said. Pangilinan said greater access to Japan could encourage investments in local agricultural production, processing and value-adding activities, generating economic opportunities for farmers, workers and small businesses throughout the agricultural supply chain. He underscored the global competitiveness of Philippine agricultural products, citing bananas, mangoes, pineapples and coffee as among the commodities with strong export potential. “With the quality and abundance of our agricultural products, our farmers and fisherfolk should not be limited to supplying food within the country. They should also become participants in the global food supply chain because our products, such as bananas, mangoes, pineapples, coffee and many others, are world-class,” he said. However, the senator emphasized that making the Philippines a stronger exporter would require sustained government assistance and trade policies that allow local products to compete more effectively in international markets. The proposed tariff exemptions seek to cover certain agricultural commodities under the Japan-Philippines Economic Partnership Agreement (JPEPA), which provides for the reduction or elimination of tariffs on more than 90 percent of goods traded between the two countries. Pangilinan said expanding export opportunities must go hand in hand with policies that enable Filipino farmers and fisherfolk to benefit directly from international trade. The Philippine Senate delegation, led by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, met with Japanese government and parliamentary officials, including Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, former prime minister Fumio Kishida and Japanese Senate President Masakazu Sekiguchi. The delegation held engagements with the Japan International Cooperation Agency, the Japan-Philippines Parliamentary Friendship League, the Japan-Asean Inter-Parliamentary Exchange Group and other institutions to explore ways to strengthen bilateral cooperation. Japan is a major destination for Philippine agricultural exports, particularly bananas. In 2024, the Philippines shipped approximately $635 million worth of bananas to Japan, accounting for more than 1.1 million metric tons and maintaining its position as the country’s leading banana supplier. The existing trade relationship underscores the potential for expanding shipments of other Philippine agricultural products, including mangoes, pineapples, coffee and other high-value commodities. However, despite the JPEPA, which took effect in 2008, certain agricultural products continue to face tariffs and other market restrictions. The agreement provides preferential trading arrangements, including tariff reductions and exemptions, but concessions vary depending on the commodity. Fresh bananas, for example, have continued to face import duties in Japan, prompting Philippine agriculture officials to seek their removal. In October 2025, Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. raised the issue with Japanese officials, seeking the elimination of tariffs on fresh Philippine bananas and improved market access for pomelo. He noted that banana tariffs could reach 18 percent, potentially affecting the competitiveness of Philippine shipments against suppliers from other countries. Apart from tariff barriers, Philippine agricultural exporters must also comply with Japan’s stringent food safety, phytosanitary and quarantine requirements. This makes investments in modern farming practices, postharvest facilities, cold-chain infrastructure, processing and product certification essential to ensuring that more Filipino farmers can participate in the export market. The Philippine Statistics Authority reported that agricultural exports reached $9.25 billion in 2025, a 19.3-percent increase from the previous year’s $7.75 billion. However, the country continued to record an agricultural trade deficit of $11.12 billion, underscoring the need to strengthen domestic production while expanding opportunities for locally produced commodities in international markets.

articles.title: EU age assurance study finds privacy risks manageable, costs relatively low
articles.desc: The European Commission has published an independent study examining the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and the costs for businesses implementing it. The document follows up on the recommendations of the co-chairs of the Special Panel on child safety online, which urges the EU to intr
articles.content: The European Commission has published an independent study examining the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and the costs for businesses implementing it. The document follows up on the recommendations of the co-chairs of the Special Panel on child safety online, which urges the EU to introduce “fundamental rights-respecting age assurance requirements to better protect children online.” The new report carries that work forward, examining how rights-respecting age assurance could be “operationalized in a future EU legislative instrument.” This is based on the observation that, “while support among broader stakeholders is far from universal, there is emerging political consensus on the proportionality of age assurance as a policy approach, when it is undertaken in a manner that is rights-respecting.” Thus, the need to examine the critical question of “how precisely age assurance can be implemented in a manner that is rights-respecting.” Privacy, non-discrimination, access to information are key rights Author Owen Bennett’s analysis centers on three fundamental rights – the rights to data protection and privacy, to non-discrimination, and to freedom of expression and access to information – arguing that these are the rights “most directly engaged by the deployment of age assurance” policies and systems. Core suggestions are that risks to these rights could be mitigated through “strict enforcement of the GDPR, the leveraging of privacy-preserving deployment architectures, and a focus on choice and optionality.” While it raises concerns around the risks that come with age assurance – the possibility of discrimination and exclusion, the potential limiting of kids’ right to access information – and underscores the need to accept those realities, it ultimately adds to the growing body of literature supporting the argument that effective, proportionate and rights-preserving age assurance frameworks can be achieved. ‘Clear avenues’ for mitigating risks The feasibility of fundamentally rights-respecting age assurance frameworks stems in part from the availability of tools to curb risks. The GDPR, Bennett argues, must be the lodestar for legislative coherence, and data protection authorities must have the resources needed to enforce it. The importance of strict compliance with the GDPR is an overarching theme throughout. Moreover, “the development and adoption of technical standards that establish privacy and security baselines for the age assurance sector” could further mitigate risk. The paper notes how the perceptual impact of age assurance systems can lead to less access generally, potentially infringing on the right to free speech. “The reality of having to assure their age more frequently might dissuade some of-age individuals from using online services or, if they are unable to assure their age using the available methods, might lead to them being locked out of services.” “Furthermore, public suspicion that an age assurance mandate is the first step towards generalized online identification and surveillance infrastructure might likewise push of-age users away from online services, or engender a chilling effect in how they express themselves and seek information online.” Minimizing friction, maximizing choice and prioritizing “meaningful communication and clear transparency” are the proposed ways to mitigate these risks. (Although “clear communication and meaningful transparency” would perhaps have been clearer.) Cost of deployment low, while per-check cost to decline over time Of particular note for biometrics and identity firms offering age verification or age estimation products is the section on financial impact. Age assurance requirements “invariably introduce novel costs” for service providers. That makes cost a major factor in competitiveness, alongside time. “The age assurance sector is increasingly competing on ease of integration, with vendors advertising integration timelines of days or less, and offering ready-made plugins for common website builder platforms like Shopify and WordPress,” the paper says. “Deployment costs should therefore be low for the great majority of services, and cluster around the hundreds of euro or the low thousands. Service providers that seek to build and deploy proprietary in-house age assurance systems would incur far higher costs – likely in the hundreds of thousands of euro.” For most online services, third-party age assurance vendors therefore appear to offer a considerably cheaper route to deployment than building proprietary systems. Ongoing service costs “bifurcate into operational costs and per-check costs,” the latter of which tend to reduce with volume. “While costs vary depending on the method used, implementation data regarding the UK age assurance mandate estimates that the per-check cost incurred by services has a median of around EUR 0.07, with most checks falling at or below a cost of EUR 0.12.” That number is higher than some of the estimates cited by the Age Verification Providers Association – but not by much. Operational costs include compliance, information security and user support, and “will likely scale in proportion to the number of age checks that a service provider performs.” As such, “reliance on third-party age assurance solutions that bundle these services, or the leveraging of existing corporate capabilities in functions such as information security and user support, could meaningfully ease the increased cost burden.” Costs are likely to trend downward over time, as the technology and its deployment advances, and mutual recognition initiatives allow costs of age assurance to be shared across participating service providers. EU age verification blueprint faces deployment gap Bennett's assessment of the EU's age verification white label/blueprint – or app architecture for tokenized age assurance – is that while it has the potential to be “among the cheapest available compliance pathways for service providers of every size,” deployment remains low. Bennett recommends accelerating the roll-out of the blueprint across all Member States; permitting and encouraging deployment approaches that reduce friction and per-check costs, such as successive validation, reusable proof-of-age attestations, and interoperability; and leveraging “the growth of technical standards for the third-party age assurance sector, to reduce costs associated with vendor due diligence for service providers.” Legislative and policy tools exist to support viable, rights-respecting ecosystem In conclusion, the paper asserts it has shown that “age assurance poses interferences with the fundamental rights to privacy, data protection, and freedom of expression, and carries foreseeable risks of discrimination and exclusion. In terms of scalability, it also creates novel costs and compliance burdens for service providers, large and small alike.” But both the risks and costs are manageable with “deliberate legislative design and policy implementation” that prioritizes privacy and transparency. Ultimately, Bennett concludes that, should the EU decide to introduce dedicated age assurance requirements, “there is a clear path by which the European Commission can make age assurance rights-respecting and proportionate in its deployment.”

articles.title: Arunachal minister inaugurates geothermal drying unit, seeks clearance for seismic microsonation project
articles.desc: Itanagar, Nov 10 (IANS) Arunachal Pradesh Science and Technology Minister Dasanglu Pul on Tuesday inaugurated a geothermal-powered drying unit at Dirang in West Kameng district, marking a significant step towards harnessing renewable energy for agricultural development and improving farmers' livelih
articles.content: Itanagar, Nov 10 (IANS) Arunachal Pradesh Science and Technology Minister Dasanglu Pul on Tuesday inaugurated a geothermal-powered drying unit at Dirang in West Kameng district, marking a significant step towards harnessing renewable energy for agricultural development and improving farmers' livelihoods. The facility, funded by the Union Ministry of Earth Sciences with additional gap funding from the Arunachal Pradesh government, was inaugurated in the presence of Norwegian Ambassador to India May-Elin Stener, Dirang MLA and Advisor to the Minister Phurpa Tsering, and scientists and experts from India, Norway and Iceland. Addressing the gathering, Minister Pul said the initiative would help translate scientific research and technological innovations into practical solutions for the benefit of farmers and rural communities. She added that the facility would utilise natural geothermal heat to dry and preserve locally produced agricultural and livestock products, including kiwi, apples, persimmons and yak meat. Custom Ad: Multiplex The technology would help minimise post-harvest losses, enhance the market value of locally produced commodities, increase farmers' incomes and create sustainable livelihood opportunities, she said. Pul, who also chairs the Centre for Earth Sciences and Himalayan Studies (CES&HS), appreciated the technical cooperation extended by Norway and Iceland in setting up the facility. During her address, the Minister urged the Union Ministry of Earth Sciences to issue the formal sanction order for the already-approved Seismic Microsonation Project in Arunachal Pradesh. Highlighting the state's vulnerability to earthquakes, she said the project was particularly important as Arunachal Pradesh falls under Seismic Zone-V, the country's highest seismic hazard classification. She added that the proposed project would strengthen disaster preparedness, facilitate scientific assessment of earthquake risks and support safer infrastructure planning across the state. Pul also expressed gratitude to Chief Minister Pema Khandu for his continued encouragement and support for scientific innovation, research and sustainable development initiatives in Arunachal Pradesh. Welcoming Norwegian Ambassador May-Elin Stener on her maiden visit to the state, the Minister expressed hope that the geothermal drying initiative would pave the way for greater international cooperation in renewable energy, scientific research and technology transfer. The event was also attended by Ministry of Earth Sciences Scientist-G and Advisor Jagvir Singh and Oil India Limited Director (Exploration and Development) Soloma Yomdo. Pul congratulated CES&HS Director Tana Tage and his team, Oil India Limited and the international partners for their contributions to the successful implementation of the project. Emphasising the importance of making scientific advancements accessible to ordinary people, the Minister said the true success of science lay not merely in achievements in laboratories but in translating research and innovations into tangible improvements in people's lives. --IANS sc/khz
